explanation: Fires on whitespace in hard-wrapped or column-aligned text: a newline that breaks a sentence mid-clause in wrapped prose, a ' *' or '//' continuation marker at the start of the next line of a license comment, or a run of padding spaces in tables and aligned code. It is strongest when the sentence obviously continues past the break. Ordinary words and paragraph breaks at the end of a sentence give little or nothing.

No single theme. It fires strongly on function words and pieces inside all-caps legal case captions ('UNIT[ED] STATES', 'WRIT [OF] CERTIORARI', 'IN [THE] COURT'), on 'on' in 'released/arrested him on', on the '.expect' method chain in Rust, on pieces of foreign or rare words, and on quote or '="' tokens in config code.

Fires on the token that completes a stock phrase or multi-word name and is highly predictable from what comes before: 'Redistributions' in BSD license lists, 'Continue [reading]', 'Tony [Award]', 'Peace [Corps]', 'all over the [globe]', 'Reader [of] field'. Tokens that are not predictable continuations stay weak.

A mixture. It fires on 'for' in the counsel lines of legal opinions ('..., Atlanta, Ga., [for] respondent'), on verbs and pronouns in legal filings ('filed [his] petition', 'he [contends]'), on subword pieces of brand or technical names (Ples[k], m[agento], CL[IA], V[PS]), and on a scattering of ordinary prose words.

Mainly fires on the second or later token of a multi-word proper name or place, where the first word sets it up: 'South [Sudan]', 'University of [California]', 'Los [Angeles]', 'East [Asia]', 'Trans[-Pacific]'. A second job is the slash-plus-piece token in compounds and units ('transfer[/c]opy', 'micromol[/l]'). Other tokens are weak.

Fires on the first subword piece of a rare, foreign or technical word that the tokenizer splits into several pieces: ' transf'(obo), ' nucle'(ocapsid), ' Vir'(at), ' Analy'(se), ' K'(GB), ' Ab'(strium). This holds across many languages and in names. Whole common words fire weakly.

A mixture with no shared theme: pieces of identifiers in Java/F# import lines (Buffer[Strategy]), word pieces inside proper names (Tec[mo], Mack[enzie], Fog[hat]), digits inside years, ZIP codes and citation numbers, CSS property pieces, and some function words.

Fires on the end-of-line token (newline, '.
', ',
', '");
') inside a source file's header comment block (license, copyright or 'auto-generated' notices) where the next line starts with a comment marker ('//', '#', ' *'). The same kind of line end in ordinary code or prose fires weakly.

Fires on the first token at the start of a new line, especially when that line continues the text before it (a lowercase word such as 'and', 'of', 'at', 'i', or a word piece) after a hard line break or blank line. It also fires on the first token of a line in legal documents and code. Tokens in the middle of a line are weak.

Fires on prepositions, articles and nouns in the middle of descriptive or expository clauses ('cast [as] a single piece', 'influence [to] perform', 'the [RAM] of another', 'the [men] slogged'). There is no clear lexical or contextual trigger that would predict it.

Fires on the first subword piece of a long or technical word that is split into fragments, most strongly ' Att' in 'Attorney/Attica' (often in legal captions) and ' enc' in 'encroachment/encrustation/encircling'. It also fires on biochemical word pieces (glycosamin[og]lycan, neo[ant]igens, oste[ocal]cin) and German or Finnish compound pieces.

Mostly fires on separators and digits inside dotted or numeric identifiers: the dots in IP addresses and OIDs, digits in port numbers and statute citations, '=' in error codes, '-' in version strings. It also fires on assorted word pieces in names and chemistry ('d[ith]iothreitol') and on some unrelated prose words, so it is mixed.

The main job is the ' (' that opens an abbreviation right after a spelled-out multi-word scientific term ('vasoactive intestinal peptide [(]VIP)', 'norepinephrine [(]NE)'), plus the hyphen in such compounds. A second job is package-path pieces after 'import' in Java/Kotlin ('import [io].gitlab...', 'org.n[extr]tc').

A mixture. It fires on emphasis or negation adverbs before a verb ('to [really] watch', 'to [actually] get', 'may [not]', 'can['t]'), on commas after a name or place in biographical appositives ('Born in Suzhou[,]'), and on a few connectives ('so [that]', 'for').

Fires on a heterogeneous set of mid-sentence tokens: 'subject [to]', '[that]' after 'said on Wednesday', commas after introductory phrases, '[said]' after 'A spokeswoman', pieces of identifiers and chemical names. No common feature is apparent.

Often fires on the head word that completes a software or technical name or compound noun ('Android [Studio]', 'Visual [Studio]', 'xcode [project]', 'free [utility]', 'financial [incentive]', 'Node-[RED]'). Many top examples are unrelated function words, numbers and file-name pieces, so it is not a clean concept.

Fires on tokens in French-language text: function words and word pieces in French prose and in French code comments ('[qui]', '[a] indiqué', 'Quelqu['un]', '[l]'éditeur'). It also fires on indentation before XML tags in French files. Weaker offshoots are 'United' in legal or UN names and some code punctuation.

Fires on nouns that name a sports or recreation playing surface or venue: lawns, courts, golf course, swimming pool, pitch, home ice, baseball field, track, rinks, runway, stadium. It is strongest when the sense is the physical playing area. The same words in non-venue senses ('fields of electric appliances', music 'tracks') are weak.

Mostly fires on subword pieces in the middle of uncommon words and names (Pfle[ider]er, Marie [Cou]vent, Beg[otten], th[ym]idine, pyrote[chn]ic, carp[ent]ers). It also fires on short variable tokens in code ('= [rev]', '[r].RoleName', ':[not]()'), so it is partly mixed.
Fires on scattered tokens: function words, commas before quoted speech, word pieces, and nouns, across science, sports, lyrics and code comments. There is no discernible common trigger.

Fires on tokens in sysadmin, systems or developer-infrastructure text (servers, filesystems, databases, emulators, build paths), especially the '.m'/'-m'/'=s' style piece that joins a domain, file extension or platform name ('cve[.m]itre', 'x64[-m]ingw32', 'md4[.m]4', 'rootfstype[=s]quashfs'). A second job is prepositions and articles describing server setups ('tablespace [on] a different drive', 'behind [a] load balancer').
